newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto citing corruption.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto citing corruption.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari sacked Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday, accusing her government of widespread corruption and nepotism.
It was the second time Bhutto has been sacked.
Army units took over key installations in Islamabad at about 2 a.m. (2100 GMT Monday) after the order was issued, but there was no sign of any major restriction on movement of traffic in the capital.
The official news agency APP said the president had ordered general elections for February 3 and had appointed former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid, as interim prime minister.

"Corruption, nepotism and violation of rules in the administration of the affairs of the Government... has become so extensive and widespread that the orderly functioning of Government in accordance of the provisions of the Constitution and the law has become impossible and in some cases, national security has been endangered.
"Public faith in the integrity and honesty of the Government has disappeared," he wrote in a proclamation issued by APP.

In a sweeping indictment of her three-year old stewardship, former Bhutto ally Leghari cited what he said was her failure to stop the extrajudicial killing of thousands of people in Karachi and elsewhere.
He also accused her of undermining the presidency and the judiciary, of phone-tapping and eavesdropping, and of failing to reconsider the sale of national oil and gas assets.

"I am satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Federation cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the constitution and an appeal to the electorate is necessary," he wrote.

Bhutto has been in power since general elections in October 1993, her second spell as prime minister after then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her for similar reasons after 20 months' rule in 1990.
The president has constitutional powers to dismiss elected governments and dissolve parliament's lower house.
Bhutto's spokesman Farhatullah Babar said Bhutto had received a letter from the president between 1.30 and 1.45 a.m. (2130 and 2145 GMT) at her official residence in Islamabad.
"She is at her house but is not receiving any calls at the moment," he told Reuters by telephone. He said he expected Bhutto to react publicly later in the day, but gave no details.
Asked if there had been any military deployment, he said: "No, no such thing."
